Input: Which animal species on Earth consists only of one gender? None of them, because other animals don't have genders. This may seem like I'm splitting hairs, but it's an important enough topic that it's worth knowing the distinction. Gender and sex are not the same thing. Sex is purely about biology. Gender is a cultural construct. Very few other animals have culture in the first place, and among those that do, we haven't seen any evidence of gender roles in the same way as human culture, and certainly not any single gender cultures as this question is asking for. Granted, you can find plenty of pop-sci articles and sometimes even legitimate research that treat 'gender' and 'sex' interchangeably, but that's sloppy use of language, not validation of mixing up those terms. I came across an article that explains all this much better than I could, so rather than make this answer unnecessarily long, I'll simply provide that link for more information:

Is it considered rude to be served on paper plates and plastic utensils at a dinner party? It depends on the formality of the party and the number of guests. But even then, there are other options besides paper plates. If it's hot dogs and hamburgers from the grill, paper plates are fine. If it's prime rib, roasted potatoes, and grilled asparagus, you'll probably want to serve those on something nicer. If it's a small enough dinner party to where you own enough plates to cover it, go with real plates with real silverware. But if the party gets bigger than that, then it's just a practical matter that you have to do something else. We do this every Christmas and Thanksgiving with my wife's family. She has a pretty big extended family, so these are meals for several dozen people. But we still don't go with paper plates. We try to compromise with 'nice' disposable dinnerware. Something like this, which is actually plastic plates, plastic utensils, and a plastic wine glass: ABOVE SOURCE: Sam's Club But some other family events get hosted by family members not quite as concerned about 'formality'. So then it might be paper plates and regular plastic utensils. And, well, taking the time and spending the money to provide a meal for the whole family is generous enough. Rude would be turning up your nose at that meal because the dinnerware wasn't fancy enough. Basically, if you're doing the hosting yourself, try to use dinnerware that matches the formality of the meal, even if it's disposable. If you're attending an event that somebody else is hosting, appreciate the generosity even if it is paper plates.

If you are an atheist, how do you explain conscience to yourself? As for YOU, where does it come from? Our innate morality is an evolved instinct as a social animal. Depending on the conditions and the niche, social groups can offer animals synergistic benefits greater than the sum of the individuals. So, you see various levels of social cooperation in all types of packs, herds, tribes, troops, pods, etc., with ants and bees being some of the most extreme examples. Individuals living in such social environments need social instincts, not just to make the group successful, but, and this is the really important part in regards to evolution, so that they're accepted into the group so that they can take advantage of the group benefits for themselves. If you ever watched the show Meerkat Manor, you may recall that meerkats kicked out of the group had much, much worse chances of survival than meerkats living in the group, so there's a very strong selection pressure for meerkats to have instincts that keep them in the group with all the benefits that provides. But it’s not a hippie dippie love fest. There are also conflicting instincts to not be too selfless to the group, lest an individual sacrifice their own reproductive success. Conversely, all members of the group have an interest in identifying and punishing freeloaders and cheats, since they would drag down the success of the group as a whole. Along those same lines, individuals will have an interest in not doing things that would mark themselves as cheats, themselves, to avoid punishment. So, social animals evolve a whole range of complex and sometimes conflicting impulses to maximize their success in such settings. Even actions that go against their own short term self interest may be important in maintaining their long term acceptance within the group. Of course, most of us aren't so Machiavellian and calculating in our own behavior and internal thought processes, but, anthropomorphizing what is in fact a mindless process, natural selection was when it instilled those instincts in us. And so that brings us to where we are today. Perhaps it's easiest to understand the impulses towards selfishness and nepotism for the more direct benefits they would seem to bring us and our offspring. But empathy and conscience are just as important for social animals, since they're critical to our acceptance into social groups and the benefits we get from living in those groups. Note: This answer was adapted from a previous answer: I'll also note, that in the interests of brevity, I didn't even get into topics like kin selection, which add another layer of reasons to cooperate and have feelings of empathy.

How is it possible that every little detail required for life and the human species to exist on Earth just happened to happen naturally? There's probably somewhere on the order of 100 billion planets in the Milky Way galaxy, with all types of varying conditions. Just by chance, some of those planets will be conducive to life, while others won't. But guess where the intelligent life is going to be, wondering why their planets just so happen to be so well suited for their evolution. Just say that "every little detail required for life and the human species to exist" on a planet is a one in a million chance. With 100 billion planets, that still means 100,000 planets in our galaxy with those conditions. Even if it's a one in a billion chance, that's still 100 such planets. We don't yet know enough about planets outside our own solar system to say how rare it is for such conditions to exist. But even if it is extremely rare, it just stands to reason that the organisms pondering such things will be on the life supporting planets. And of course, we evolved to fit our planet, not the other way around. If other planets harbor life but with slightly different conditions, that life will almost certainly follow a different evolutionary path, producing creatures that don't resemble us humans. Also, this is an extremely self-centered question. You might as well ask how Earth is so conducive to tapeworms, or mushrooms, or oak trees. I rather like humans myself, but we're not the end-all, be-all of life on this planet. Heck, by biomass, the Earth really is a planet optimized for microbes, with us multicellular creatures just adding a bit of variety to the fringes.

If “burger” now includes fish and chicken sandwiches instead of only ground meat patties, what is the boundary between burgers and other sandwiches? In American English, 'burger' on its own most certainly refers to a ground beef patty on a bun. You can stretch the definition a bit by adding a description of some other ingredient besides beef, such as a chicken burger or a veggie burger, but the implication is that it's still a ground food of some sort formed into a patty. For example, this is a chicken burger. Note the ground chicken formed into a patty: ABOVE SOURCE: Natasha's Chicken Burgers While this, since it contains a whole piece of chicken that's been breaded and fried, is a chicken sandwich: ABOVE SOURCE: The OG Chick-Fil-A Sandwich Where you can run into a bit of a gray area is a ground beef patty that's not on a bun. If you put the patty in between two slices of grilled bread with cheese, then it's a patty melt. And then it's just a question of semantics as to whether or not you think a patty melt is a type of burger or something separate. The article I copied that image from does refer to it as a specific type of burger, and I tend to agree since the defining feature of a hamburger (with it’s origins from a Hamburg steak) is the ground beef patty. ABOVE SOURCE: This Is Why Whataburger Patty Melts Are So Delicious - Mashed Yes, I know that in some other countries, practically anything on a bun is referred to as a burger. I was a bit surprised (and relieved) one time going to a get together with my German friends, when they said they were going to make chicken burgers, but they were actually making what I would call chicken sandwiches. So to answer your question, in American English, the boundary between a burger and other sandwiches is using a ground meat (or veggie) patty. No patty – no burger.

Some people say Jesus didn’t resurrect but was resuscitated by Joseph of Arimathea, after which he lived secretly in other parts of the world till the age of eighty. If true, why didn’t the apostles know about this and allegedly died as martyrs? I've seen a few of these ideas with a mix of skepticism and credulity, where they're skeptical of the divinity of Jesus and the supernatural aspects of the stories, but they still treat the overall accounting of events as a fairly reliable narrative. Other similar ideas I've heard include Jesus only being in a coma, or disciples secretly stealing the body. But why? If we already think that the gospels are unreliable accounts, then why accept anything in them at face value that needs any more explanation than simply saying it was made up? Now, I don't necessarily mean that all of the stories were intentional lies (though I'm not ruling it out, either). But rather, the gospels weren't written down until decades after the supposed events had taken place, by people who never met Jesus in person and were relying on oral history that had plenty of time to morph and become exaggerated in the retellings. Any stories in the gospels are just as likely (if not more so) to be urban legends or mythologizing than anything based in fact. So, assuming that there was a real Jesus at the core of this legend, and that he was indeed executed by the Roman authorities, how do we explain what happened to his body? More than likely, it was left up on the cross for a while as an example. And whenever it was taken down, it was probably thrown into a mass grave with other executed criminals and political dissidents. Whatever the inspiration for the belief in the resurrection (and I cover some possible scenarios here - Jeff Lewis's answer to What does a Quoran atheist, with a Christian upbringing, think actually happened following Jesus Christ's crucifixion?), there's little reason to trust most of the details in the gospels, and thus little reason to try to think up more rational explanations. There may well never even have been a Joseph of Arimathea in the first place. As far as apostles and/or disciples dying as martyrs, those stories are partly in the same category. The stories in the New Testament of Christian martyrs are themselves of dubious accuracy, so we really don't know just how widespread martyrdom was. And as far as it did happen, well, people believing in urban legends and conspiracy theories is hardly surprising. You can find plenty of modern day examples in just a few minutes on Facebook – even folks so committed to their beliefs that they staged an attempted coup on the U.S. Capitol, and one man who even martyred himself when he lit himself on fire in protest of a criminal trial against former president Donald Trump. People within echo chambers and cults can build themselves up to committing extreme actions that those of us on the outside find shocking and irrational. In short, there's no reason to spend undue effort trying to rationalize all the different details in the gospel stories, when perhaps the most likely explanation of most stories is urban legends and mythologizing that grew over the decades the stories spread as oral history. But just like in the modern day, there were at least some people who did very much believe in those urban legends, probably enough to lose their lives over those beliefs.

👋 Hello. Although I have many reservations about the New Testament, I wonder why so many people put pen to paper about the life of Jesus. What inspired them to write about his life. Surely there is a 'Kernel ' of truth contained within them? I guess there are two shades of meaning to this question. Why did people write about Jesus at all (which I'll cover first). And why did so many people write about him in particular, to the relative exclusion of similar cult leaders at the time (which I'll get to a bit later). Broadly speaking, people were motivated to write about Jesus for the same reasons that they write about anybody. I've discussed a more modern day cult leader here on Quora before, Sathya Sai Baba*. He just died relatively recently in 2011, and you can find a ton of stuff written about him by his followers, from an official biography, to innumerable online essays by rank and file followers. You can even find answers by many of his followers right here on Quora (just type his name into the Quora search bar). Whatever you might think of his own motivations (e.g. were his 'miracles' intentional sleight of hand deception), he struck a chord with people and was able to parlay that into fame and a successful movement in his lifetime. Will Sai Baba's cult survive for centuries like Jesus's did? Who knows? Some sects seem to die out with the death of their leader, while others seem to resonate even afterwards. There are plenty of examples of this persistence, from major religions right down to smaller sects – Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, Mormons, Seventh-day Adventists, Rastafarianism, Scientology, etc. I don't think there's really any way of knowing why Jesus's cult became so hugely popular compared to all the other similar cults in that time and place. Heck, history has relegated John the Baptist to basically supporting cast in the Jesus story, despite being a leader of a religious movement in his own right.** There have actually been studies on smaller scale versions of this. Back in 2003, some researchers created a music download website that they could control to run experiments. They tested a specific set of songs across multiple groups. None of the groups could see what songs the other groups had downloaded or how the other groups rated all of the songs. So in each group, there was equal opportunity for any song to go 'viral'. And what they found that was it was probabilistic and random at the same time (stochastic). Some songs tended to end up in the top downloads more often, while other songs tended to remain relegated to the bottom, but the specific songs that became the most popular varied from group to group with no way to definitively predict it ahead of time. It seemed to come down to random chance and extreme sensitivity to initial conditions. Here’s a pop-sci article discussing the study, and the actual research report: So, there probably was something to Jesus's message about loving your neighbor, caring for the poor, and not being judgmental that resonated with people. But why that particular cult ended up becoming a major world religion as opposed to the similar cults is probably down to chance. Had history played out a bit differently, billions of people might now be worshipping John the Baptist, wearing necklaces with dinner platters instead of crucifixes. * That previous answer about Sathya Sai Baba can be found here: ** It’s interested to read Josephus’s mention of John the Baptist, where he describes John the Baptist as an important figure in his own right, not some second fiddle to Jesus like in the Gospels:

What do you do when your kid says that they are sick but you think they are faking it? I was pretty lucky growing up, in that I think my mom had hated school just as much as I did. So she was pretty lenient about letting me stay home "sick". To be fair, I never completely faked it, but I did embellish and play up minor headaches that I wouldn't even think twice about as an adult and still going to work. So, I tried to extend the same courtesy to my own daughter when she was still at home and in school. As long as she kept up with all her schoolwork and still got good grades (which she always did – to brag just a bit, she graduated as salutatorian*), I never pried too much into just how "sick" she really was. If she wanted to stay home for the day every once in a while, I let her. *Technically, I was a valedictorian, myself, but our school didn't do weighted averages or anything else to break the tie. I don't remember the exact number, anymore, but we had something like 20 valedictorians – not exactly super prestigious.

Why is the left so adamant in their denial that COVID-19 came from the Wuhan virology lab? It's like a chocolate flood in Hershey, Pennsylvania. Might it be from the candy factory? Let's start off with the likelihood of where the pandemic originated before getting into the politics. First, although I realize that appeals to authority aren't a strictly logical argument, expert opinion is still a very useful heuristic. These are folks who have in depth knowledge and expertise on a topic, and much more likely to have a well informed opinion than a random stranger on the Internet. And the natural animal origin (zoonotic origin if you want to get technical) is the clear consensus. That's not to say that a lab leak is impossible. It just seems much less likely at this point, especially among the folks who have devoted their careers to studying such things. ABOVE: Results of a survey of 168 virologists, infectious disease epidemiologists, and other scientists SOURCE: The Origin and Implications of the COVID-19 Pandemic: An Expert Survey | Global Catastrophic Risk Institute (click through to the PDF report) I also came across a very informative debate about the issue. If you have a half hour or so, I'd really recommend reading the whole thing: I think the two pieces of evidence that I found the most convincing had to do with the original cases. They were centered around the wet market in Wuhan, not the Wuhan Institute of Virology: ABOVE SOURCE: Practically-A-Book Review: Rootclaim $100,000 Lab Leak Debate And even more specifically, the cases within the market were centered around a racoon dog vendor, an animal which is a known carrier of COVID-19: ABOVE SOURCE: Practically-A-Book Review: Rootclaim $100,000 Lab Leak Debate In fact, two years before the pandemic, a scientist who was visiting that very same market took a picture of the conditions of the racoon dogs, because he was told even back then that "This is the kind of place that has the ingredients for cross-species transmission of dangerous pathogens." ABOVE: Conditions of racoon dogs and birds in the wet market back in 2014 SOURCE: NPR IMAGE CREDIT: Eddie Holmes As that debate I linked to put it: People say it would be a surprising coincidence if a zoonotic coronavirus pandemic just so happened to start in a city with a big coronavirus research lab, and this is true. But it would be an even more surprising coincidence if a lab-leak coronavirus pandemic just so happened to first get detected at a raccoon-dog stall in a wet market! The other piece of evidence concerning the first cases has to do with the two separate early lineages of COVID-19, Lineage A and Lineage B. Lineage B is the one centered specifically in the wet market. But even Lineage A was first found in a neighborhood nearby the market. Quoting that debate once more: Again, it would be a bizarre coincidence if a lab leak pandemic was first detected at a wet market. But it would be an even more bizarre coincidence if a lab leak pandemic separated into two strains, and both were first detected at a wet market! Another strong piece of evidence is that COVID-19 seems most likely to have evolved from a related coronavirus, BANAL-52. But BANAL-52 wasn't discovered until after the pandemic, once interest in the origins of COVID-19 had spiked and people were trying very hard to determine where it came from. It's hard to study a virus in a lab that you haven't discovered yet. Of course, there's plenty more detail to it than that. Like I already said, I'd highly recommend reading that debate I already linked to. Here's another good, somewhat shorter article from a few years ago, and a podcast that I've heard is good (but I prefer reading to listening to podcasts, so I haven't listened to it myself): [ETA - Here’s another good link I just ran across:] None of this is to say that the natural origin is 100% likely, or that the lab leak has a 0% probability. But it certainly does seem like the natural origin is the more likely explanation. Okay, so what about the political aspect of it? I'd like to say that it's because 'my' side of the aisle is always rational and evidence based, and so they're just following the science. And there's certainly a troubling strain of anti-intellectualism and anti-science infecting the Republican party right now, as I explained in a previous answer (Some worry that the United States is in an unusually anti-intellectual period right now. Is this really the case? Haven't societies always been composed mostly of people who are rather unthinking and just want "bread and circuses"?). But as I also noted in that answer: I'm a bit cynical about the Democratic support of science. While I'd love for it to be authentic, I suspect it's mostly virtue signaling in opposition to the Republican distrust of science. But at least lip service in support of science is still better than organized opposition. In other words, I suspect many folks on the left are so adamant in their support of the natural origin of COVID-19 not because they understand the science, but because so many people on the right seem to support the lab leak hypothesis, and so this issue, like so many others, has become divided along party lines, and a way to advertise your allegiance to your own tribe. But just to return briefly to the main point of this answer – the evidence really does point to a natural origin of COVID-19 as being the most likely explanation. Maybe not 100% certain, but more certain than a lab leak.

Do atheists believe that cucumbers could evolve into kangaroos if given enough time? Well, I'm not going to say it's flat out impossible, but it does seem very, very unlikely. This is a great example of how historical contingency constrains evolution, since that's not at all the way us animals evolved in the first place. Here's an evolutionary tree of eukaryotes, which is the group that includes both us and plants. Land plants, which includes cucumbers, are in the top left, while us animals (metazoans) are in the bottom left: ABOVE SOURCE: https://bsapubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.3732/ajb.1300314 This figure also shows multicellularity vs. unicellularity vs. colonial species. Based on the pattern, it appears that multicellularity evolved independently in several lineages. Or in other words, our common ancestor with plants was still unicellular, and that we and plants each took a different path to arrive at multicellularity. The lineage that led to plants had already developed photosynthesis before evolving multicellularity, so all of their development towards multicellularity was geared around that lifestyle. Likewise, our single celled ancestors were already consuming other organisms, so all of our development towards multicellularity was geared around that lifestyle. And at this point in the present, our different lineages are specialized for our respective lifestyles. What's more, they're not particularly compatible lifestyles. While sunlight is very plentiful, it's not particularly energy dense compared to eating other organisms. So, plants get by on a lot less energy than us animals, which is part of the reason they tend to be generally immobile (though you do get occasional fast responses like Venus fly traps). By contrast, when we eat a plant, we're basically getting all that energy the plant has stored up over time in just a few bites, before going on to the next plant and the next plant, so we can spend much more energy on things like moving around (not that animals have to move around, as evidenced by sponges). For something like a cucumber to evolve into something like a kangaroo is a drastic, drastic change in how those organisms make a living. Sure, if I get creative enough, I can think of kinda sorta plausible scenarios where it could happen, but truth be told, they don't actually seem genuinely plausible. What's more, as long as existing animals are around, you've got to worry about the competitive exclusion principle. What incipient animal-like plant would be able to outcompete existing actual animals? So yeah, given enough time, I'm not sure you could completely rule out something like this, but it does seem rather unlikely.

If could put a space plane in a 100km high orbit, would the small amount of lift move it in to a higher orbit? Look at it this way. If you had a normal plane at a normal altitude and cut the engines, do you think the plane will start going higher because of the lift? No. Because airplanes also have drag, and that drag will rob the aircraft of energy. Without the thrust from the engines, the only way to maintain speed is to use gravity to descend. If a space plane were in orbit to where there was enough atmosphere to create a non-negligible amount of lift, it would also create a non-negligible amount of drag. That drag would begin to slow the space plane down. That in itself would be enough to make the plane begin losing altitude because of the way orbits work (you’re always falling, it’s just that your horizontal velocity keeps you moving sideways fast enough that you keep on ‘missing’ the ground). If you did want to maintain your speed without using engines, you’d have to descend even faster.

Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump? Yes. And Trump could beat Harris. Presidential elections in the past 30 years have all been relatively close. Roughly half the votes will go to either candidate, plus or minus a few percent that decides who will win (and a few more percent to third party candidates). And of course, that whole process gets filtered through the electoral college, so a candidate doesn't even need a majority of the popular vote to win the election. ABOVE SOURCE: United States presidential election - Wikipedia This year will be no different. Trump will get around half the vote. Harris will get around half the vote. Whoever performs best in the swing states will win the overall election. Sure, you've got plenty of people right now making 'guarantees' about who will win. And given that it's really a binary choice, a lot of those people will inevitably end up picking the eventual winner. But it doesn't mean they actually had any better insight than the rest of us. It means they just got lucky by calling the coin toss. I think we can safely predict, at least, that Robert Kennedy is not going to win. Side note: I don't mean to discount polling as worthless. I think it still is useful and valid as long as you understand it's limitations. It's just that polling can't tell you much when elections are decided by less than the polling margin of error. Another side note: This question is from 2016, but for obvious reasons, it's taken on a new found relevance.

Think of a small submarine 10 miles deep in the ocean, 1 gallon of water now drives a generator at 80k PSI, then energy is used to separate hydrogen from water and moved to the surface for use. Any holes in this thought experiment? I don't see any 'holes', per se. It just doesn't seem practical for any real world purposes. If I understand the description in the question, you'll end up with something like this on your sub: You've got a tank big enough to allow 1 gallon of sea water to drive a turbine to generate power, and that power will be used for electrolysis to create hydrogen and oxygen. Pressure can be thought of as energy per volume: So, just rearranging a bit, energy is pressure times volume. You need some type of pressure differential to get any work out of that, which is why the contraption has that tank at atmospheric pressure in the diagram above. But since atmosphere pressure is so much lower than the water pressure that deep, we can just assume it's negligible. Anyway, assuming everything was 100% efficient (which it won't be), using the correct value of 16k psi for the pressure in the deepest part of the ocean, and that I’ve done all my math properly, that 1 gallon of water has a potential energy of 308k ft-lb or 0.156 hp-hr, or in terms more familiar to folks who aren't U.S. based engineers, 418 kJ or 116 Wh. In contrast, a AA battery has roughly 3.9 Wh. So your device, at most, has the potential to generate as much energy as 30 AA batteries. In actuality, after all of the efficiencies are accounted for, it will be even less than that. I think your sub is going to need more than 30 AA batteries worth of energy to complete its mission, so you're spending more energy to perform this mission than what you get out of it. So, while this device could theoretically generate hydrogen in principle, there are far more practical ways of generating power.

How was the 2024 solar eclipse? Was there much of a panic/emergency as the USA prepared for or just a fizzle? The thing about preparing for potential emergencies, is that if you do your job well and avoid any problems, then everybody wonders what the fuss was about in the first place. The legitimate concerns around this eclipse (outside the conspiracy theories on Facebook) were mainly centered around so many people coming together in one area – things like traffic jams or strains on the supply chain (particularly food and fuel). Such concerns were based off the prior experiences of the 2017 eclipse. A report on traffic conditions, for example (TR News - Traffic Impacts of the 2017 Solar Eclipse), found that at least 5 million people had traveled to view that eclipse, that nearly all the Interstate highways in the path of totality ended up red on Google Maps immediately after the eclipse, and that some trips that would normally only take 4 hours by car actually took 13 hours in the wake of the eclipse. So, in preparation, some locations pre-emptively declared a state of emergency to be better able to address such concerns, or to be able to mobilize the National Guard for extra manpower just in case they would be needed, or made sure that highway related positions were all fully manned (e.g. toll booths, rest stops, emergency vehicles, etc.). Traffic did still turn out pretty bad in some places (there’s only so much you can do without changing the infrastructure), but I haven't heard of any major incidents or problems. So were officials over-prepared? Or did they just do a good job and help curtail any problems before they happened?

Can a jet break windows if it breaks the sound barrier far away from the building but then it flies by it? I think I see the misconception in the way you worded the question. A sonic boom isn't a one time event that occurs just at the instant an airplane surpasses the speed of sound. It's a shockwave that trails behind the aircraft the entire time it's flying faster than the speed of sound. When pressure waves move out away from an object, the wavefront is a sphere expanding at the speed of sound. That's basically what the speed of sound is, since sound is itself pressure waves in air. As long as you're below the speed of sound, those pressure waves can expand faster than the aircraft is moving. But once you hit the speed of sound, those pressure waves can't expand out faster than the aircraft is moving, so they pile up on the front side, creating a 'wall' of high pressure air known as a shock wave . As the aircraft flies even faster than the speed of sound, this shockwave trails behind the aircraft in the shape of a cone. This conic shockwave travels along with the aircraft. When it passes you by, that sudden increase in pressure is the sonic boom. So, it doesn't matter how long ago the aircraft first exceeded the speed of sound. It matters how fast it's going when it's flying over you. If it's supersonic, it will still be creating that shockwave, and you'll still experience the sonic boom as the shockwave passes you by. In reality, with all the different parts of an aircraft sticking out into the air, you'll have multiple shockwaves coming off of the aircraft. But with those shockwaves being so relatively close together, and the aircraft flying so fast, you'll experience them all combined as one event.

Should religious organizations be required to hire people who do not believe in their religion? It depends on the circumstances. In general, no. If it's a purely religious organization focused on purely religious pursuits, then the First Amendment is clear, and if they want to hire only religious folks, they're free to do so. If, however, it's an organization that drifts into more secular pursuits, things can get trickier. The issue is that bigoted folks can try to use religion as an excuse to avoid the same laws that apply to everyone else. Are they sincerely religious, or are they just using religion as a cover? Does it matter? I know that things have changed in the largest Mormon denomination, but up until the 1970s, racism and segregation were baked right into official church doctrine. Would it really be fair to let, say, a homeless shelter or a food bank discriminate against black people because the people running it didn't want needy black folks mingling with needy white folks? Personally, I don't think so. I think that a homeless shelter or food bank are moving enough away from religion and into secular pursuits that they should have to follow the same laws as everybody else. I know. The above isn't a perfect example for this question since it addressed who the organization served, not who the organization hired, but I think it's still helpful. Basically, if the scope of your organization is purely religious, then you can discriminate against people outside your religion as much as you want. But if your organization starts moving beyond religious pursuits into the broader world, at some point you'll be expected to follow the same rules as everybody else, and not fall back on your religion as an excuse for bigotry.

WWII two boomers had 4 engines and could get back on 2 or even 1 engine. Why don’t commercial passenger aircraft have 4 engines for increased safety? Because while 4 engines provide more redundancy, they also provide more opportunities for things to break. Plus, when designing any mechanical system, there's no such thing as 100% perfectly reliable, so you have to balance how reliable is reliable enough vs. other factors like cost and maintenance. Commercial airliners have settled on a safety standard commonly referred to by the shorthand of 10^-9, or to spell it out a bit more, a risk of less than 1 catastrophic failure for every billion flight hours. That's an extremely safe standard requiring very rigorous design, analysis, testing, and tightly controlled manufacturing processes. And, to put it bluntly, there's little incentive to exceed that standard, especially if your competitors aren't, because exceeding that standard will compromise other aspects of the product. I mean, if you're going to ask about installing 4 engines instead of 2, then why not 6, or 8, or 10? Each increase would provide even more redundancy. The answer comes down to reliability and maintenance. Modern engines have roughly equivalent reliability from one model to the next. So, if you install 4 engines instead of 2, it means you'll have reliability issues twice as often, grounding the aircraft for engine related maintenance twice as often. Installing 6 engines would lead to even more maintenance downtime. And of course, it gets worse and worse the more engines you install. While more engines would provide more redundancy, the airlines would be losing money because of that extra downtime for maintenance. So it comes down to the question of how safe is safe enough? And for commercial airliners, the agreed upon value is 10^-9, which is achievable with 2 engines. It's also worth noting that piston engines are nowhere near as reliable as gas turbine engines. While a gas turbine engine can acheive 10^-9 safety with just 2 engines, you couldn't with just 2 piston engines. That's part of the reason why older, piston powered airliners had more engines. Finally, add in the fact that airliners can still glide even with a loss of all engines. Perhaps the most famous example of this is the Gimli Glider. Due to a mixup in refueling, the aircraft (a Boeing 767) ran out of fuel at 41k ft, and then proceeded to glide to an emergency landing, with no serious injuries, and only minor damage to the aircraft that was subsequently repaired and put back into service. (As a side note, this is part of the mitigation for single engine piston planes, which have no redundancy and much less reliability than gas turbine engines – the fact that they can glide to an emergency landing.) When balancing safety vs. other parameters like cost, performance, and maintenance, the agreed upon standard for commercial airliners is 10^-9 safety. And with the reliability of modern gas turbine engines, you only need 2 engines to achieve that. More engines would compromise other aspects of the design.

Question for atheists- how do you feel about Christians talking about their faith with you if they are nice about it (ie not screaming that you are going to Hell)? Do Christians in this manner bother you? I hope my question makes sense. I love it. I really, really like civil debates/arguments with friends. I mean, what's the fun in just agreeing about everything all the time? Especially when it comes to controversial subjects, these types of discussions are where we truly test our own positions. Do we really have a firm foundation for our beliefs? Have we really thought things through? I mean, it would be easy to only hang out in Internet echo chambers and just pat yourself on the back amongst folks who already agree with you, but that's where you run the risk of holding beliefs for superficial reasons. It's only when you test out your arguments among people who are going to challenge you that you can be sure that those beliefs are well founded. I also realize that atheists are still a fairly small minority in this country (USA), and that there's still a fair amount of stigma towards atheists. So by having these conversations, I can help to educate the person I'm talking to about atheism, and help de-stigmatize atheists. I can think of plenty of folks who were shocked to learn I was an atheist, because the stereotype of atheists in their mind was based on straw men and falsehoods. And just maybe, I'll plant some seeds of doubt about Christianity, helping them to see the light and embrace reality rather than ancient superstitions. I don't mean to imply that this is all one way street with me talking down to the Christians. It does me good to remind myself that not all Christians are like the con-men, hucksters, liars, and bigots that get so much publicity like Kent Hovind, Joel Osteen, Jimmy Swaggart, Benny Hinn, Ray Comfort, Fred Phelps, Robert Jeffress*, etc., etc. No, most Christians I meet in real life are just regular folks trying their best to live good lives, but it's hard to escape childhood indoctrination and cultural pressure. And I often learn things myself from these conversations. Perhaps not as much when it comes to religion (since I've studied it more than most of the religious folks I know), but certainly with many other controversial topics I'll argue with my friends about. And of course, everything in moderation. While religion is an occasional topic of conversation amongst me and my friends, it's not the only topic of conversation. There's a whole lot more to life that we spend more time on. As a real life example, just a few months ago, I had a couple Mormons show up in my driveway. They told me a little bit about their beliefs. I told them a little bit about the documentary hypothesis to explain the origins of parts of the Bible, and how Yahweh had developed from previous traditions within Canaanite polytheism. I'm not sure I convinced them of anything, but at least they knew I wasn't some stereotype who called myself an atheist merely because I was angry at God. It was all nice and friendly, and we were smiles and handshakes as they left. So yeah. I love conversations like these when they do happen. They're how we challenge ourselves and each other to be sure that our beliefs are well founded and robust, and they help to remind us that people who disagree with us on certain topics are still just regular folks. *I almost feel a bit guilty about Jeffress, since he used to head up a Baptist church here in Wichita Falls, where I live. Even though I never supported him while he was here, I still feel a tiny bit of guilt by association, that somehow we unleashed him on the rest of the world.

As a non-Christian, do you have any questions or anything I can clarify with you about Christianity/the Bible? Skimming over your profile and responses to other questions, you seem to have asked this question in good faith, so I'll respond in kind. Starting at the beginning, the first creation account in Genesis does not match the actual history of the universe and our planet that we've learned through geology, astronomy, paleontology, etc. Now, I've heard some folks argue for a day-age interpretation to try to reconcile the creation story with reality, but that still has issues with things not being created in the right order (e.g. day, night, and plants all being created before the Sun, birds being created before land animals, etc.) So how do you reconcile the first creation account in Genesis with reality (or do you)? And assuming the story is divinely inspired, why would a god inspire such a misleading story in the first place? Related to that, the two creation accounts in Genesis contradict each other, with the 7 day creation account telling a different story than the Garden of Eden story. It appears nearly certain that's because they come from different traditions, the Priestly source for the former, and the Yahwist source for the latter. In fact, there are at least four sources for the Pentateuch, the two already mentioned, along with the Elohist source and the Deuteronomist source, not to mention the Redactor who edited them all around the time of the Babylonian Exile (more info: How Was the Bible Formed? - Bible Odyssey and What Is Source Criticism? - Bible Odyssey). While the discrepancies between sources are clear in the two different creation accounts, there are plenty of other discrepancies throughout the books. Even for a common story told in two prior traditions like Noah's flood, you get interweaving of details, like different durations for the flood, and different numbers of animals to take on board. So again assuming that the Bible is divinely inspired, why would a god take such a tortuous route to assemble it from all these various prior sources, and why leave so many contradictory details? What about the polytheistic origins of Yahweh and the Bible? You said questions about the Bible, so I'll leave out archaeological questions (like the Kuntillet Ajrud Inscriptions). But what about Deuteronomy 32:8–9: 8 When the Most High[b] apportioned the nations, when he divided humankind, he fixed the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the gods;[c] 9 the Lord’s own portion was his people, Jacob his allotted share. This seems very much to come from a prior tradition where Yahweh was still considered one of many gods. There's also the story in 2 Kings 3, where it seems very much that King Mesha's sacrifice of his firstborn son to his god (unnamed in that particular story, but it was Chemosh) granted the Moabites favor to win the battle: Then he took his firstborn son who was to succeed him and offered him as a burnt offering on the wall. And great wrath came upon Israel, so they withdrew from him and returned to their own land. How do these polytheistic passages fit into a conception of Yahweh as the one and only God? And echoing the prior question, why assemble a divinely inspired book from such prior traditions that didn't agree with the final message in the now canonical Bible? Anyway, that'll do for now. I've got plenty more questions, but this is long enough.

Hypothetically, let's say there is a world where Christianity is backed by mountains of evidence and all the stories of the Bible are verifiable and proven, would you still follow the teachings of Christianity or choose to live your own life? The problem is that this literally isn't possible. The Bible contains many, many contradictions, so you simply can't verify and prove all of the stories. The best you can do is verify some of the stories. And at that point, we're left to cherry pick which stories and lessons we want to say are proven in this hypothetical scenario. Just to go with one example, are we going with the God of Exodus 20:5-6, who threatens "punishing children for the iniquity of parents to the third and the fourth generation," or the God of Ezekiel 18:19-20, who says that "A child shall not suffer for the iniquity of a parent nor a parent suffer for the iniquity of a child; the righteousness of the righteous shall be their own, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be their own"? Because the former seems quite barbaric and not at all worthy of worship. The latter at least seems fair. Still, though, the overall portrayal of God in the Bible is not particularly flattering. You've got the massacre of Noah's Flood with its drowning of infants and children, the horrific treatment of Egyptian commoners and their slaves in the Exodus story (Jeff Lewis's answer to Can you cite the verses of some morality flaws in the Bible?), and then the whole fiery furnace of Hell for the grave sin of doubt. And that's just scratching the surface. So, given all the contradictions within the Bible, even as a hypothetical, you can't imagine a scenario where all of it was proven true. But even going with the overall general portrayal of God in the Bible, he's not a being deserving of worship.

What is the reasoning behind atheists thinking it's illogical to believe in god? Should people be allowed to have their own beliefs without being challenged by others? Let's take your latter two questions first: Should people be allowed to have their own beliefs... Yes without being challenged by others? Absolutely not. This is the type of delicate little snowflake mentality that so many people complain about. All beliefs should be robust enough that they can withstand inspection. If they're not, then maybe they weren't such good beliefs in the first place. Now, I'm not saying life needs to be one continuous debate during all waking hours. There's a time and place for everything, and there's a difference between debate and badgering (or to make a verb of a different animal, sea lioning). But yes, you should at least occasionally have discussions with people who disagree with you about challenging topics – politics, religion, morality, pineapple on pizza, etc. If you never challenge yourself, you'll never grow. And if you limit yourself to echo chambers of only like minded people, you'll never truly understand the wider world and why different people do things differently from you. I can think of plenty of examples from my own life where I'm grateful to the people who challenged me and helped me to see things differently. As far as your first question, well, that could be an entire book. But the short of it is, all the evidence we do have for God and Christianity is best explained as a mythology that developed out of previous mythologies. Heck, we even have evidence of Yahweh's origins in the Canaanite pantheon as a storm god – NOT the one and only God and creator of the universe. Other religions and their holy books are largely similar in that they've developed over generations as mythology. And the other big, glaring problem that they all have is a complete lack of credible evidence. Oh sure, Hindus, Buddhists, Christians, and Muslims all get warm fuzzy feelings when they pray, and some even manage to convince themselves that unlikely events and coincidences are evidence of their particular god(s) (but obviously, not the other gods). But this evidence hardly ever seems credible to outsiders who don't already share their beliefs. So there you go. We think it's not reasonable to believe in gods in general because there's no good evidence, and the capital G God in particular because the evidence we do have shows that he's a product of human myth making. And while we all certainly have a right to hold any beliefs we want, we should also be open to being challenged about those beliefs. That's the only way we grow as individuals.

Do pro-choice people at least think we should reduce the number of abortions? That's a weird question. It's about like asking if we should reduce the number of bypass surgeries for clogged arteries. On the one hand, as the old saying goes, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. It would be great if we could get people to live healthier lifestyles to avoid clogged arteries and the need for bypass surgeries in the first place. But as long as people do have clogged arteries, I very much want bypass surgery to be available. I don't want to reduce the number of bypass surgeries if the need still remains. And it still remains a fact of life that clogged arteries will happen regardless, so some amount of bypass surgeries will always be necessary. It's similar for abortion. It would be great if everybody had comprehensive sex education and easily available contraception and birth control to reduce the number of accidental pregnancies. And it would be great to have generally good living conditions for all families, easily affordable and accesible prenatal care, or at least adequate social safety nets, so that nobody was worried about having the means to raise a child with a good quality of life and opportunities. And it would be really great if there were no more rapes, developmental abnormalities, or other complications with pregnancies. So of course it would be nice to reduce all the reasons for abortions in the first place. But I don't want to reduce access to abortions while the need remains. And it's still a fact of life that some amount of abortions will always be necessary, because we never will fully eliminate all those reasons. So yes, like with any other healthcare issue, it would be best to reduce the causes that lead to needing medical intervention. But as long as the need's still there, you still provide the healthcare. And it's just a weird way to phrase a question, asking if we want to reduce a specific medical procedure, rather than addressing the causes that lead to that procedure.

Is English considered a foreign language to the US? Why can't most Americans speak English fluently or even close? As someone who has been learning English for about 3 months, I probably speak much better English than most Americans. Why? I'm going to focus on this part of your question: As someone who has been learning English for about 3 months, I probably speak much better English than most Americans. No, you don't. I studied Spanish pretty extensively in high school and college, to the point of being only 2 classes away from a Spanish minor*. I could speak fairly fluently. Then, after I graduated, I met the woman who was to become my wife, who happens to be Mexican with a large Mexican family (all living in the U.S.). I could catch them making grammatical 'errors' that weren't 'proper' Spanish**, and I could definitely spell Spanish words better than them (they mostly grew up in the U.S., so didn't have much formal education in Spanish). But my way of speaking Spanish was much more academic and stuffy, and just didn't flow the same way. Nobody would have confused me as speaking better Spanish than native speakers who had been speaking it their entire lives. Going the other way, I once made a business trip to China, and during the one day we set aside for sight seeing, I was approached by an old Chinese guy who wanted to speak to me in English, who turned out to be a retired English teacher. In other words, he was such an expert in the English language among the Chinese that he was teaching others how to speak English. But his English wasn't exactly the best. Don't get me wrong, his English was far better than my non-existent skills in Chinese, but it seemed obvious that he'd probably never been outside China and gotten to practice with actual native speakers. Even a lifetime of academic study isn't enough to make someone speak as well as a native speaker. Now, I really suspect you're a troll and not somebody who just began studying English 3 months ago. But people who aren't native speakers have to study a long, long, long time to become as proficient at the language as native speakers. And it really requires immersion in the culture, hearing the language day in and day out to pick up all the nuances and informalities that you simply can't completely learn any other way. On the off chance that you really are new to studying English, learn a bit of humility like I did when I met my wife’s family. Academic English is not the way real people speak, and it’s going to take a lot more than three months of studying in a school environment before you sound natural. *The reason I didn't just tack on two more classes was because I was already taking one Spanish class my final semester, and another two would have given me a very full load. So, instead, I tacked on a semester of Italian to learn a bit more of a different language. I figured the actual skill would serve me better than an additional piece of paper. **I put grammatical 'errors' in scare quotes, because I've come around to the idea of grammar being descriptive, not prescriptive. Who gets to decide what's proper and what's not. Where do they get off thinking they have that authority? Language has been around for far longer than scholars to study it, and people did just fine.

What's your go-to healthy snack when cravings hit? Single serve bags of potato chips: Because let's be frank. When it's an honest to goodness craving, rabbit food just isn't going to cut it. I see a bunch of other answers here trying to promote 'healthy' snacks, and while all those would be fine under normal circumstances when you’re merely peckish, they're just not going to satisfy a craving the same way junk food will. And I've tried. You eat the healthy alternative, and you're not satiated. You just want more. And if you eat enough until you're full, you've just eaten more calories without actually satisfying the craving. But a single serve bag of potato chips is only 1 oz of food, and only 160 calories. Sure, it's not the best thing to eat all the time. But every once in a while? That's not going to kill you. And it will actually satisfy your craving with all that starchy, greasy, salty goodness. And the fact that it's in a single serving bag makes portion control that much easier. With a full size bag, it's easy to just keep going back for one more chip, one more chip, one more chip, until eventually you've eaten a lot more than you should have. But if you know the one small bag is all you get, you eat your one serving and stop. The whole point is that a healthy diet is all about balance and moderation. And abstinence will just lead to worse cravings, or even falling off the healthy diet altogether. No single food in moderation is going to be all that bad for you. Just make sure to balance it out with enough other types of food to have a healthy diet overall. On days when the cravings aren't quite so bad to give in to potato chips, my next go-tos are pickles and olives (or olive salad on crackers). You still get enough saltiness to help satisfy the craving (and the olive oil from the olives), but not too terrible on the calories. After that is probably pita chips. Still starchy and salty, but not quite as greasy as the chips.

If the weight of a body in water is 12N and weight of liquid displaced by the body is 8N, then what is the weights of that object in air? This is a bit of a trick question. To overcomplicate it a bit, here are free body diagrams comparing when the object is underwater vs. above water (with the force arrows obviously not drawn to scale): Weight is the same in each case. And of course that has to be the case, since weight is defined as W=mg. As long as the mass didn’t change, and you’re conducting these experiments from roughly the same location on Earth (so that g doesn’t change), the weight won’t change, either. Sure, if you wanted to be very precise about the net force, you could calculate the exact buoyancy force (hint: you should know or at least be able to look up the densities of water and air). But given that water is roughly 800 times denser than air, you know that the buoyancy force from air is going to be pretty negligible. Weight doesn’t change even when other forces are acting on an object. Buoyancy may change the net force, but not the weight.

According to the Bible, the earth is only 6000 years old. How does it explain the 4.49-billion-year gap between that and the actual age of the earth? Whenever questions like this pop up, poor Archbishop James Ussher is sure to unfairly come under fire for supposedly inventing the roughly 6000 year old age of the Earth out of some misconceived eccentric interpretation of the Bible. But really, that was a fairly mainstream view of the Bible at the time. While no passage in the Bible gives an explicit date for creation, if you take certain passages at more or less face value, you can come up with a reasonable estimate. Plenty of other scholars besides Ussher came up with their own estimates, and they all clustered around the same ages – either around 5500 BC if using the Septuagint as your basis for scripture (i.e. the Greek Old Testament), or around 4000 BC if using the Masoretic Text (i.e. the authoritative Hebrew version). Wikipedia lists many of these other scholars in its article on Dating creation, and it includes such well known names as Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius of Caesarea, Hillel, Johannes Kepler (yes, that Kepler), and Martin Luther, among many more. You can get a good part of the estimate pretty easily yourself by looking at just a handful of passages: The first two list genealogies from Adam down to Abraham, including the ages of how old the men were when their sons were born. The third states that Abraham was 75 years old when he left Haran for Egypt. The four is an explicit statement of the time the Israelites spent in Egypt before the Exodus, and the fifth is an explicit statement of the time passed from the Exodus until Solomon’s Temple. And that right there is enough to get you from creation to the Bronze Age in roughly 3000 years. Sure, there are a couple ages in there that are slightly ambiguous (particularly Noah and Terah), and also a bit of ambiguity about how long it took Abraham to travel from Haran to Egypt, but you're only looking at a few years of ambiguity there, nothing major. After that is where things get more intricate. You have to scour through the reigns of a bunch of kings of Judah and piece together that history (particularly from Judges, Kings, and Chronicles). And of course, that's exactly what Ussher (and all those other scholars) did, totaling up to around 430 years. That gets you to the accession of the Babylonian king Amel-Marduk, which from other historical sources was known to have taken in place in 562 BC. So, take the 3000 years from Adam to Solomon's temple, the 424 years of kings reigning in Judah, and 562 BC as a reference point, and you end up with a date for creation right around 4000 BC (4004 BC per Ussher). Now, I'm not a believer in the Bible, myself, so I take all this with a grain of salt since I don't think the Bible is a reliable source of history (particularly the older books like Genesis). But for those folks who do take the Bible seriously, this all seems perfectly reasonable. If you want to argue that the Bible doesn't indicate that creation took place in roughly 4000 BC, which of those portions are you willing to say is wrong? The reigns of rulers in Judah? The Exodus story? The otherwise boring and tedious recitation of fathers begetting sons? Given the mainstream view in Ussher's time of trusting the Bible to be historically accurate, I think he made a pretty good go of it. He just made the mistake of using an unreliable reference. (In fact, it’s precisely because he was so diligent and meticulous in his efforts that his particular estimate became one of the most respected in his time, and why it’s still remembered today.) As far as the OP's question about reconciling this age with the more accurate 4.5 billion year age of the Earth, I think the simple answer is that the Bible was a compilation from a more primitive people who simply didn't yet know any better. They certainly weren't dumb. It just takes time for humanity as a whole to build up our knowledge, generation by generation. As the saying goes, we only know as much as we do today thanks to standing on the shoulders of giants. Related:

Do atheists actually believe they are monkeys? Do they have an urge to climb trees? Is it sad to only believe in one’s self? Let's take these one at a time: Do atheists actually believe they are monkeys? Meh. It's a semantics issue. I'm definitely an ape. And I'm definitely a primate, and definitely a mammal. And on and on for all the various larger taxonomic groups we're included in. But whether or not you think we're monkeys comes down to whether you think monkeys are a monophyletic, paraphyletic, or polyphyletic group. You can debate it, but it doesn't change the reality of the animals we evolved from. (FWIW, I have come around to thinking monkeys should be monophyletic, and that us apes are just a slightly specialized branch of monkeys.) ABOVE: Aegyptopithecus, which was a close cousin to our ancestors, and thus would have been very similar. SOURCE: Aegyptopithecus (note: the above image itself is valid, but Reptile Evolution is a bit of a dubious site - David Peters started off as a decent paleoartist, but kind of went off the deep end a couple decades back) Do they have an urge to climb trees? When a particle collides with an antiparticle, they are transformed into energy, Is it true that matter is annihilated and destroyed? Is this literally true? Matter is destroyed? Doesn't this completely contradict the law of conservation of matter? Scientific laws aren't exactly ironclad dictates that apply across all conditions throughout the entire universe. They're short expressions or formulas that are useful as long as you understand their limitations. Take Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation, for example. It's extremely accurate at the scale of everyday interactions in our lives. It's still accurate enough to predict the orbits of most of the planets to within the precision of our ability to measure them. But it's not quite accurate enough to predict the orbit of Mercury, given Mercury's close position to the Sun. For that, you need Einstein's updated theory of gravity, General Relativity. But even though we know Newton's law of gravity isn't perfect, we continue to use it since it's still plenty useful and accurate for many applications. Another law that I used quite regularly in my own field of aeronautical engineering is the Ideal Gas Law. We know for an absolute fact that real gases don't behave exactly the same way as this law. But for the pressures I normally deal with for aeronautic applications, it's good enough: It's the same thing with the Law of Conservation of Mass. It also is extremely accurate at the scale of everyday interactions in our lives, enough that many of us engineers use it for things like designing airplanes or balancing equations for chemical reactions. But we also know that it's not accurate over all conditions. As Einstein famously pointed out, E=mC², based on the fact that mass and energy are fundamentally the same thing, and can be converted from one to the other. And while this applies to everything, the difference in most everyday situations is negligible (a warm can of soda will be ever so slightly more massive than when it was cold, but your kitchen scale isn't anywhere near sensitive enough to measure the difference). So, the issue is that you're trying to apply the Law of Conservation of Mass to a condition outside where it would be valid. Instead, you need to look at the broader law, Conservation of Mass-Energy. Keeping it to still simple terms, this basically boils down to: E 1 + m 1 C 2 = E 2 + m 2 C 2 If m2 < m1, it just means that E2 has to be increased to compensate. But the total value on each side of the equation has to be the same. Nothing is being lost or destroyed, just converted.

How exactly did ancient humans defend themselves against large carnivores such as the short-faced bear? Don't think of humans as some special case that needs a special explanation. And our social groups were especially tight knit compared to most other mammals. But that doesn't really change the fundamentals.
